name: Public Enfilade
description: Formal rooms in a line with their doors aligned, so that a view runs the length of the house and a party can move through it in order. It is a device for making a modest house feel large and for choreographing an evening: receive, dine, withdraw.

internal_rules.statement: Doors align on one axis so the view runs through. A single offset door breaks the enfilade and it cannot be recovered with finishes.
Rooms diminish or grow in one direction, never alternate. Hierarchy has to be legible as you move.
Each room in the sequence is also reachable from the hall or passage, so the enfilade is a choice and not the only route. An enfilade that is the sole circulation makes every room a corridor.
Openings are wide — 5 to 8 ft with pocket or double doors — or the sequence reads as a row of doorways rather than a run of space.

attaches_to.position: one side of the passage, both rooms
the full depth beside the hall — the townhouse case, and the reason a narrow row house feels generous

attaches_to.note: The open plan is the enfilade with the walls removed, which gains the view and loses the ability to close any of it.

expansion_logic: Add a room at either end. The sequence tolerates lengthening and not interruption.
servicing_strategy: Fireplaces on the party wall or gable in the townhouse case, which stacks the flues and keeps the window wall free.

style_variation.note: Where American practice takes it furthest, often with an oval or apsidal room in the run.
Double parlours with sliding doors — the enfilade reduced to two rooms and a very large opening, and it works.
Explicitly rejected. The bungalow's open plan is an argument against ceremony, not a cheaper version of it.

sources: Waterman, The Dwellings of Colonial America
